item.title: Pentagon reveals secret space weapons are already in orbit — but won't say what they do
item.description: Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed the Space Force has on-orbit space control weapons, but the Pentagon won't say what they are or how they work.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. has weapons orbiting Earth that can be used to defend American forces from attacks in space, the Air Force secretary revealed this week in a rare public acknowledgment of capabilities the Pentagon has largely kept secret.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday that the Space Force now has "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action," but declined to say what the weapons are, how they work or when they were deployed.

The carefully worded disclosure marks a shift in how openly the U.S. military talks about weapons in orbit as China and Russia develop their own capabilities to disrupt, disable or destroy satellites.

TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY

"Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?" Meink told reporters after his remarks at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland — right outside of Washington, D.C.

"For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space," he continued. "We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment."

Exactly what the U.S. has put into orbit remains a mystery.

The U.S. has previously discussed placing weapons in space, including plans to deploy space-based interceptors capable of destroying incoming missiles as part of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense system.

But Meink’s disclosure goes a step further: The Space Force already has weapons in orbit for "space control," a mission aimed at protecting U.S. access to space and, if necessary, denying an adversary the ability to use it.

The Pentagon has historically revealed little about the weapons developed for that mission, with publicly known U.S. counter-space capabilities largely based on the ground.

"What the U.S. is going for is a wow factor here," Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. "Wow. The U.S. has never talked about space weapons like this before."

"That's really what is exceptional and newsworthy about this revelation," Swope said. "The U.S. is saying we're putting weapons in space to make sure that our adversaries can't use space, or to make sure that we can continue to use space."

Meink appeared to make clear that the ambiguity surrounding the weapons is intentional. He told reporters his language was "very well thought out" and declined to say whether the systems are kinetic or non-kinetic. Kinetic weapons physically strike or destroy a target — think bombs, bullets and missile — while non-kinetic systems can disrupt or disable it without blowing it up — like cyber attacks or radio jams.

"There are a lot of factors that roll into how we talk about these things," Meink said, explaining that publicly revealing a capability can contribute to deterrence while disclosing too much about it can undermine that advantage.

"We’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else," he said. That leaves a wide range of possibilities.

Fox News Digital did not hear back from the Space Force when reached for details of the weapon.

INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH

Swope said "space control weapons" could encompass everything from kinetic systems capable of firing missiles or projectiles at another satellite to jammers that interfere with satellite communications or lasers designed to temporarily overwhelm imaging sensors.

"We really don't have enough information to know precisely which one of these types of capabilities we're talking about," Swope said. "It's really anybody's guess what type of weapon we're talking about."

FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS

But whatever the Pentagon has deployed, putting a weapon in orbit rather than launching it from Earth could offer one potentially significant advantage: speed and surprise.

A weapon launched from Earth toward a satellite could potentially give an adversary warning that an attack was underway. A capability already positioned in orbit could dramatically shorten that window.

"Maybe something measured at dozens of minutes could be compressed into just mere minutes," Swope said.

"And you wouldn't have any indication that maybe a jammer was turned on, on the satellite, other than all of a sudden your signal is being interfered with," he added.

"If you can act fast without your adversary knowing, if you can have surprise, that gives you a strategic or an asymmetric advantage in combat," Swope said. "And having systems in orbit do just that."

Even observing the spacecraft itself may offer few clues about what it can do.

"Space is a very transparent place," Swope said, noting that governments and civilian observers can track where satellites are, how fast they are moving and what orbits they occupy.

"But what you'll see often is, oh, it's a satellite," he said. "It's a lot of technology with solar panels and antenna on it. And you don't really know much beyond that."

A satellite equipped to jam another spacecraft’s signals, for example, might look much like an ordinary communications satellite.

"Any signal can be a jamming signal," Swope said. "It just depends on if it's the one you want to receive, or the one that someone's trying to use to jam you."

The concept of weapons operating in orbit is not new. Swope pointed to the Soviet Union’s work on co-orbital anti-satellite weapons dating to the 1960s. Russia has continued developing counterspace capabilities, including systems designed to operate in orbit near other satellites.

China has also developed and tested technologies that could threaten spacecraft, including satellite-servicing and debris-removal systems that have legitimate civilian uses but could potentially be repurposed to interfere with another satellite.

Other forms of interference are already widespread.

"When we talk about jamming and spoofing and cyberattacks against space systems, these happen all the time, both from Russia and China and other countries like North Korea and Iran," Swope said. "There is so much jamming and spoofing happening around the world right now, it's almost ubiquitous."

Those attacks can target systems such as GPS and satellite communications without physically destroying a spacecraft.

That distinction could become critical during a conflict. Jamming, spoofing or cyberattacks may remain below the threshold that prompts a major military response, while physically destroying a satellite could represent a significant escalation.

"If you drop a bomb on a satellite ground station or you shoot a missile at a satellite in space, that's a big difference," Swope said. "That's a huge escalation."

The stakes are particularly high because modern U.S. warfare is deeply dependent on space-based systems for communications, navigation, intelligence, missile warning and targeting.

"Space is an enabler of joint operations," Swope said. "We can't do military operations the way that we do them today without satellites, without systems in space."

China increasingly faces the same dependency, making control of space potentially decisive in a conflict between the two powers.

"Whoever has space and can deny that to their adversary has a huge asymmetric advantage in a conflict," Swope said.

"China depends on space as well, and their use of space for joint operations looks very much like the United States," he added. "Both countries, I would go so far as to say, depend on space to conduct military operations on Earth."

item.title: German tennis star takes a jab at Trinity Rodman & losers try to cancel Ella Langley over old hunting photos
item.description: Ella Langley faces online backlash over old deer hunting photos, while Trinity Rodman rushes to the US Open and Aryna Sabalenka's fashion sparks debate.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Wow, the Dolphins are really bad.

We're not talking the usual levels of Miami Dolphins bad. We're talking about 1–15 bad, à la 2007. Except it'll be 1-16 now. If they're lucky to squeak out that one W at all.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But you know what? I'm at peace with it.

As a lifelong Dolphins fan, I'm accustomed to sadness, disappointment and misery. That's because every year when Week 1 rolls around — despite knowing better — I delude myself into thinking "this season will be better!"

I'm like Amy Klobuchar wearing the same dumb shirt and the same goofy grin.

This year, I have no such delusions. Every week, I fully understand the team will s---- itself worse than that HYROX chick. Only this time, instead of a quarterback who gets concussed every other week, we have one who runs fast and wears rhinestone cleats.

Ah, the serenity of low expectations. I'm as carefree as Bo Nix.

So with that, let's get to our Tuesday Nightcaps — featuring Trinity Rodman, Ella Langley and Aryna Sabalenka.

And there will be nothing about Sydney Sweeney, Holly Rowe or Arch Manning. Because I'm tired of hearing about all of them.

Let's roll.

Some people really don't like Ella Langley.

I've heard a multitude of reasons for this: She cut a song with Morgan Wallen. She followed Charlie Kirk on TikTok. She got some lip filler. She's allegedly MAGA.

The real reason is probably because "Choosin' Texas" has spent a bazillion weeks at No. 1, and a good chunk of our population just likes to hate on people who are successful.

But now, the miserable souls of the interweb have found a new reason to smear the good name of Ella Langley — she's a hunter!

Some folks with too much time on their hands dug up some old photos of Ella showing off bucks she harvested in her home state of Alabama.

I love how that second post said she'd been "caught" hunting animals. As if Ella didn't pose for that photo and post it on her own social media account.

Damn, you really busted her!

Let's see what the comments are saying.

Very sane people over there on the Twitter machine.

As the founding mother of OutKick OutDoors, I'm obviously pro (legal and humane) hunting and fishing. And I won't bore you with all the reasons why hunting — particularly whitetail deer hunting — is crucial for conservation, preventing the spread of disease, and funding for the protection of wildlife and their habitats. I encourage you to do your own research if you're interested in learning more.

JORDAN DAVIS FACES FAN BACKLASH OVER HAWAII AXIS DEER HUNT DESPITE STRONG CONSERVATION BACKING

I also have no problem with people who choose not to hunt or choose not to eat meat. That's absolutely your prerogative.

But I guarantee at least 99% of the people screeching at Ella right now have no problem stopping by the Taco Bell drive-thru or picking up a pack of chicken at the grocery store. But harvesting your own fresh venison apparently makes you evil.

Spare me the outrage, losers.

Trinity Rodman is a world-class soccer player for the USWNT. But she's also a tennis WAG.

So while her boyfriend, Ben Shelton, competed in the US Open the past couple of weeks, Trinity was in the stands supporting him.

Unfortunately for Trinity (and America), Shelton lost to Germany's Alexander Zverev in the men's final. That's after she played a soccer game in Washington, D.C. on the same day and then rushed 200 miles to NYC to catch the end of the match.

When he won, Zverev gave Trinity a shoutout.

"Trinity, I thought you have a game today," Zverev joked. "Well done to you as well. You’re the lucky charm ... not today, but usually."

The crowd laughed. Trinity laughed. Ben laughed.

And then Iman Shumpert wanted to see Ben defend his lady's honor.

"I ain't gonna lie, Ben, get up in there, you gotta say something. I ain't gonna lie, he just shot..." Shumpert said. "You need a rematch. Yeah, you gotta treat it like boxing. Hey, Ben, go get your get back, buddy."

Zverev might have stolen the Grand Slam title. But I don't think she's stealing Shelton's girl. She seems pretty into him.

Let's open the mailbag.

📩 Email: amber.harding@outkick.com (Send your thoughts, stories, tips, rants and photos of your dog.)

🐦 Twitter/X: @TheAmberHarding

📸 Instagram: @amberharding

...at least according to Keith H.

Keith writes: No one watches Women’s basketball and no one cares about whatever "tournament" is going on. The only things more boring are Women’s hockey, Women’s soccer, and watching paint dry.

Amber:

Folks, Keith cares so little about women's basketball that he clicked on a story about the USA women's basketball team's semifinal game against Spain. Then, he found the writer (me) and typed out an email about how much he doesn't care. On a Saturday night. While college football was on.

Going to such lengths suggests to me that Keith actually cares a lot about women's basketball.

Listen, folks, the reason we cover so much WNBA is because our women's basketball coverage consistently performs spectacularly well in metrics like page views, search and engagement. If it didn't, we wouldn't spend so much time and energy writing about it. All of our show hosts wouldn't be talking about it. And we certainly wouldn't send a reporter all the way to Europe to cover it.

We give the people what they want. And even the "hate reads" count as page views, baby.

A couple of weeks ago, I wrote about making my first trip to the St. Lawrence River in Upstate New York. But it certainly won't be my last.

Brian S. writes: It’s not a very manly phrase, I realize, but I was tickled pink reading your reaction to the St. Lawrence River. I was born - 1969 - and raised in Upstate New York. The River and 1,000 Islands have been a destination for my family since the 40’s. We grew up trailer camping in the state parks there, before renting cottages once we outgrew the camper, and eventually my folks purchased a summer home in Cape Vincent, a short drive from Clayton, where you were.

My now adult children looked forward to every summer stay, even though the drive from New Jersey is about 5-1/2 hours. Whenever I bring friends to the area for the first time, they all have the same reaction as you had. We may have even crossed paths last weekend, as my wife and I were there visiting for a few days, and we even checked out the Bassmasters tourney.

I’m glad you were able to experience the beauty of the region, and hope you’re able to visit again in the future.

Amber:

Every summer, my husband and I like to retreat to Lake Superior, and the St. Lawrence area area reminded me a lot of the Northwoods.

There's just something so serene about the small towns around the Great Lakes. Everything's just slower there — in the best way possible.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Lucia writes: May I ask why the uproar over Sabalenka’s choice of tennis attire, but I hear nothing about Osaka’s abysmal fashion choices. First, let’s ask why she needs an entrance ‘outfit’? They definitely say ‘look at me’, but I don’t see them as making much of a statement about her tennis skills. Secondly, Osaka’s court wear yesterday could have very easily been made out of the Hefty Bags you referenced in your article. With that said, I’m not a fan of Sabalenka’s attire either. Nike should be embarrassed they put their ‘swoosh’ on the fishnet. While she may have a contractual obligation, she and her management should have put their respective foot down.

Lastly, I don’t understand why the urge to make a ‘fashion’ statement has become a thing. Used to be the serve, the smash, the volley said it all.

Amber:

To be fair, I have seen plenty of people poke fun at Osaka's wild get-ups.

I think the entrance outfit and the non-traditional kits are just part of tennis culture right now. It's like NFL and NBA players playing dress-up just to walk from their cars into the stadium on game day.

Sabalenka's mesh kit wasn't my favorite, either. But it got us talking. And that was probably Nike's goal.

My fellow "South Park" super fans will likely agree that last season was the worst one yet.

No, not because they made fun of Trump. They made fun of Trump for five whole seasons when they had an orange-faced Mr. Garrison acting as President of the United States.

The difference is that those seasons were original, funny and clever. This past season was none of those things.

It was just Trump having a "butt baby" with Satan and the same "small d—" joke over and over and over. We get it. Even my liberal friends were like, "Can we please go back to the actual characters of 'South Park?'"

But, naturally, Hollywood loved it. So Trey Parker and Matt Stone were awarded their first Emmy.

Well, "South Park" is back tomorrow. Except they're calling it "South America" to make fun of Trump's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

And you know what? Cool. That's the kind of satire they should be doing. And judging by the trailer, it's actually going to be about the boys this time.

So, fingers crossed, this season won't just be another giant turd sandwich.

You sold out and got your Emmy, Matt and Trey. Now please go back to being funny.

item.title: Australian surfer risked his life to save fellow surfer who had been attacked by a shark
item.description: Mel Ismail lost a foot while surfing alone at Glenfield Beach in Western Australia after a shark bit his leg and took a chunk from his surfboard.
item.content:encoded:
A 56-year-old father from Western Australia faces a "long recovery" after losing his foot in a shark attack while surfing alone, 9 News Australia reports.

Mel Ismail was in the water at Glenfield Beach when he was bitten by a shark on Monday morning. In addition to biting his leg, the shark also bit his surfboard and took a chunk out of it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

"[He is] receiving specialist care from an experienced multidisciplinary team with the capability and expertise to manage complex and critically unwell patients locally," the head of the ICU department, Dr. Mary Pinder, said.

"This person remains in a stable condition; however, he has sustained serious injuries and faces a long recovery."

Ismail is lucky to be alive, all things considered. He was rescued from the water by Shannon Dunn, a fellow surfer who 9 News reports also works for the region's emergency services.

FISHING CONTENT CREATOR WHO FILMED HIMSELF BEING BITTEN BY A SHARK WHILE SPEARFISHING LUCKY HE STILL HAS LEG

Dunn was on the shore when he noticed Ismail waving for help. He didn’t hesitate. He hopped on his board, risked his life and headed towards the bloody waters. He then pulled the injured surfer back to shore.

Once on shore, some teenagers pitched in and ended up making a tourniquet out of the rope from a surfboard. Dunn then tossed Ismail into the back of his vehicle and drove him to a waiting ambulance.

Some heroes wear capes. Some enjoy surfing and also drive a Ute.

The shark attack is being investigated and authorities are telling swimmers in the area to use extra caution. A portion of Glenfield Beach was temporarily closed after the encounter.

The outlet reports that the full extent of Ismail's injuries isn't known. He is in serious but stable condition, receiving treatment at Geraldton Health Campus’ Intensive Care Unit/High Dependency Unit.

item.content:encoded:

The video in question showed the awkward postgame interview between Sarkisian and Rowe after Texas came back to beat the Ohio State Buckeyes on Saturday night. "I specifically want to apologize to Holly Rowe for what she has personally had to deal with because of my comments. I have a ton of respect for her and appreciate her showing me grace in this moment. I need to do better and will be more thoughtful going forward."

Rowe wrote on social media that she accepted Manning’s apology.

Sarkisian’s brief moment with Rowe after the game went viral.

"Texas fight, hook ‘em," he said before running back to celebrate with his team.

Overall, it appeared to be a frustrating night for Sarkisian. ESPN’s Laura Rutledge said at halftime that technical issues forced Sarkisian to wait a while before a halftime interview could begin. However, it took too long and he needed to prepare for the next half.

item.title: Retired NFL star falls into social media hole by comparing Mike Vrabel scandal and Jonathon Cooper arrest
item.description: Justin Simmons criticized ESPN for mentioning Jonathon Cooper's NFL suspension during the Broncos-Chiefs game, sparking sharp social media pushback.
item.content:encoded:
Justin Simmons was an outstanding NFL safety, collecting second-team All-Pro honors four times during his nine-year career. However, now retired, Simmons should probably be more careful with his social media commentary.

That's because Simmons stepped on something of an online landmine Monday night while he was watching his former Denver Broncos team play the Kansas City Chiefs.

During the broadcast, ESPN's Joe Buck noted that Broncos' linebacker Jonathon Cooper was not in the lineup because he's currently suspended on the NFL exempt list while he awaits a Nov. 10 trial on four charges, including felony second-degree assault by strangulation of his former girlfriend.

3 NFL STARS HIT COMMISSIONER'S EXEMPT LIST AFTER OFFSEASON FILLED WITH LEGAL TROUBLE

The broadcast apparently triggered Simmons, who took to his X account to make a comparative point.

The former NFL great complained that ESPN was mentioning his former teammate during the broadcast but the situation between New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel and former reporter Dianna Russini wasn't discussed on TV.

NBC REMINDS PREGAME VIEWERS ABOUT MIKE VRABEL-DIANNA RUSSINI SCANDAL COACH AND PATRIOTS WANT TO FORGET

So, social media simply moved on without pushback whatsoever.

Yeah, right.

Multiple people basically told off Simmons. They made the point that even if Vrabel's relationship with Russini was perhaps morally wrong, if one assumes it reached heights that have not been proven, it wasn't illegal.

Vrabel has been put before the court of public opinion for the relationship, but there are no allegations of abuse that will be heard in a court of law. The analogy between Cooper and Vrabel is flawed at best.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So, Simmons found himself in a hole he jumped into. Then, unfortunately for him, he proceeded to dig himself deeper.

"That’s absolute bs btw," Simmons wrote in an ensuing post as a media critic. "Shame on all of the production on Monday night football and the crew. You’re supposed to call the game. Coop isn’t playing the game and isn’t on the sidelines.

"The MNF crew is paid to cover THE GAME not the players who are not playing or even at the game."

That's an interesting use of capital letters. Let's go with that flow:

Simmons is apparently of the opinion that, since his former teammate isn't playing nor on the sideline – BECAUSE HE WAS ARRESTED ON CHARGES OF CHOKING HIS FORMER GIRLFRIEND AND THEN SUSPENDED BY THE NFL – the broadcast should not mention his name and situation.

So any person not in the stadium is apparently off limits from discussion, per Simmons. That apparently should include a person who would be playing if he hadn't done something for which he was arrested, charged with and apologized before he got lawyered up and pleaded not guilty.

NFL FACING A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE EPIDEMIC THIS OFFSEASON WITH ARREST OF RAMS LINEMAN THE LATEST CASE

Simmons is a bright individual of great character. He played well and was a leader throughout his career, which means he rarely faced public criticism.

He was clearly caught off guard, then, when fans challenged his views on Vrabel and Cooper and on ESPN's right to address the matter during its broadcast.

"I have hella people in my comments (mainly Pats fans) saying an affair is not the same as an ALLEGED conviction," Simmons wrote. "Which is true. However, last time I checked MNF or any network hosting a game is supposed to talk about just that THE GAME not players who aren’t there or even playing."

That is obviously not correct.

And what's worse, the premise all this is based on is also incorrect. That's because when the New England Patriots opened their season against the Seattle Seahawks, Vrabel's situation was addressed on national television.

NBC even included the Russini-Vrabel scandal in an illustrated timeline of the Patriots' offseason.

So, yes, Vrabel's situation was discussed on TV and that was the right thing to do – just like it was perfectly correct for Cooper's situation to be mentioned on Monday Night Football.

Most of us hand over a lot of personal information to the DMV because we have no choice. Your address, birth date, driver's license information and other identifying details can all end up in government systems. That is why a breach involving driver records deserves attention.

Florida officials have now confirmed that the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles, or FLHSMV, experienced a data breach. The agency says it learned about the incident on Sept. 4, quickly mitigated it and has seen no further breach or ongoing unauthorized access.

The confirmation follows claims from the ShinyHunters extortion group that it accessed Florida's Driver and Vehicle Information Database, known as DAVID, and stole more than 200,000 driver records.

Florida has not confirmed that record count or publicly said exactly what information was taken. Here's what ShinyHunters claims happened, what Florida says its investigation found and what drivers should do now.

FLHSMV says its investigation traced the breach to credentials belonging to a single Plant City Police Department user. According to the agency, those credentials were improperly stored on the employee's personal electronic device. A criminal actor was then able to take advantage of them.

That explanation gives us the first official account of how the breach occurred. It also differs from the access method ShinyHunters previously described.

FLHSMV says it notified the Florida Office of the Attorney General as required under state law. The agency is also working with the Florida Digital Service and Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The criminal investigation remains ongoing. Officials say additional information will be released at an appropriate time.

ShinyHunters says it stole more than 200,000 driver records from DAVID. BleepingComputer reported that the group provided a screenshot of a DAVID record belonging to Jeffrey Epstein as evidence that it had accessed the system. The screenshot reportedly contained an address, Social Security number, birth date, driver's license information and registered vehicle details.

DAVID can contain far more than a person's basic driver's license information. Government records describing the system show that authorized users may have access to driver information, photographs, signatures, vehicle history, insurance information and other identifying records.

However, FLHSMV still has not disclosed how many records were accessed or stolen. The agency also has not confirmed ShinyHunters' claim that more than 200,000 records were taken.

CyberGuy reached out to FLHSMV for additional comment, but did not hear back before our deadline.

ShinyHunters originally told BleepingComputer that it breached DAVID through a password-reset flaw. The group claimed that weakness allowed it to compromise multiple accounts, allegedly including accounts belonging to DMV employees and an FBI agent. ShinyHunters said it then moved through DAVID record IDs and downloaded associated pages and driver files beginning Sept. 3. The group later said it had lost access and believed the password-reset issue was being patched.

Florida's investigation now points somewhere else. FLHSMV says the attacker took advantage of credentials belonging to one Plant City Police Department user that had been improperly stored on a personal electronic device. The agency has not backed ShinyHunters' claim that a password-reset flaw allowed the group to compromise multiple accounts. So, for now, the password-reset explanation remains ShinyHunters' version of events, while compromised police credentials are the access method Florida has publicly identified.

DAVID serves authorized government users rather than ordinary public searches. FLHSMV says its Bureau of Records manages access to driver records through DAVID for law enforcement and other approved entities. The agency also audits users for compliance.

Florida policy treats personal information in motor vehicle records as confidential. That information can include Social Security numbers, driver identification numbers, addresses and medical or disability information. That kind of information can give criminals powerful material for identity theft.

Imagine getting a call from someone claiming to represent a government agency. The caller already knows your address, birth date and driver's license information. Suddenly, the scam sounds far more convincing.

IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?

BleepingComputer previously reported that a source said the attackers were targeting DMV platforms in other states through social engineering. ShinyHunters also told the outlet it expected additional DMV breaches to surface.

There has been no confirmation from Florida that the current breach involved other state DMV systems. Still, the possibility deserves attention because state motor vehicle agencies hold information that can be extremely valuable for identity fraud and targeted scams.

If criminals find a technique that works against one government system, they often look for similar access elsewhere.

ShinyHunters is an extortion operation associated with data theft attacks against companies and online services.

Threat actors using the name have been linked to attacks involving Salesforce environments and companies including Google, Cisco and Match Group.

More recently, the attackers have used voice phishing, also called vishing. In these attacks, someone impersonates IT support and tries to convince an employee to enter credentials or authentication codes into a phishing site.

The attackers have also targeted single sign-on accounts connected to services such as Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and Salesforce.

FLHSMV referred to the attacker in its statement only as an "international cybercriminal organization." The agency did not publicly identify ShinyHunters by name. So, while ShinyHunters has claimed responsibility and Florida has confirmed a breach, Florida has not publicly attributed the attack to the group.

Still, this shows why protecting trusted accounts has become so important. Once an attacker gets legitimate credentials, other connected services may become accessible too.

You do not need to wait for a confirmed case of identity theft before protecting yourself. These steps can make stolen personal information harder for criminals to use.

A credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. You need to place a freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Credit freezes are free. You can temporarily lift one when you legitimately need a lender to access your credit.

Check your credit reports for new accounts or inquiries you do not recognize. You can request your reports through AnnualCreditReport.com, the federally authorized source for free credit reports. Also keep an eye on your financial accounts. Small unfamiliar transactions can sometimes be an early warning sign.

A confirmed breach creates a ready-made lure for scammers. You could receive a text, email or phone call claiming your Florida driver information was exposed. Be especially careful if the sender pressures you to verify personal information or click a link. Instead, visit FLHSMV through its official website at flhsmv.gov/ yourself.

FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA

Scammers may use news of a DMV breach to send fake alerts containing malicious links or attachments. Strong antivirus software can help detect malware, phishing sites and other threats before they compromise your device or personal information. Keep your antivirus software running and updated on your computers and mobile devices. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Your primary email account deserves extra attention because criminals can use it to reset passwords for other services. Give it a strong, unique password and use a password manager to create and securely store it. Then turn on multifactor authentication. Whenever possible, consider an authenticator app or passkey rather than relying only on codes sent by text message.

Review bank accounts, credit cards and other important services for activity you do not recognize. Also pay attention to unexpected government correspondence. A strange tax notice or benefits letter could signal that someone has used your identity.

You may also want to consider an identity theft protection service that monitors for suspicious use of your personal information and can help with recovery if your identity is stolen. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

If you discover identity theft, report it at IdentityTheft.gov and follow the recovery steps provided by the Federal Trade Commission.

Data brokers and people-search websites can provide scammers with even more information about you. Removing that data cannot erase records stolen during a breach. However, reducing the information available elsewhere can make it harder for criminals to build a detailed profile and create convincing scams.

Consider using a personal data removal service to help find your information on data broker sites and submit removal requests on your behalf. These services can also keep checking for information that reappears over time. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

Now that FLHSMV has confirmed the breach, scammers could imitate any future notices sent to affected drivers. FLHSMV has not yet publicly disclosed how many people were affected or exactly what information was taken. Do not automatically trust an email simply because it mentions DAVID or the Florida DMV. Avoid using links in unexpected messages. Go directly to the agency's official website to verify any notice.

Florida has now confirmed the breach, but some of the biggest questions remain unanswered. ShinyHunters claims it stole more than 200,000 driver records, while Florida says the attacker got in using credentials belonging to a Plant City Police Department user that were improperly stored on a personal device. What we still do not know is exactly how much information was taken or whose records were exposed. Until Florida releases more details, I would take this seriously. Check your credit, lock down your important accounts and be especially suspicious of unexpected DMV texts, emails or calls asking you to verify personal information.

item.title: Savage bear attack leaves wounded Montana hunter with horrifying option
item.description: A severely injured Montana hunter managed to drive himself home following a brutal bear attack, officials said. Now authorities are issuing a warning to hunters.
item.content:encoded:
After a savage bear attack on Monday morning, a severely injured Montana hunter climbed behind the wheel for a desperate drive home.

In a Monday statement, Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks (FWP) said the man was hunting on state-owned land near Elk Creek and Haystack Butte, south of Augusta, at the time of the attack.

The victim was archery hunting "when he encountered the bear and was attacked," officials said.

YELLOWSTONE BISON ATTACK WITNESS BELIEVES MAN SAVED HIS GRANDSON BY TAKING BRUNT OF ATTACK

"The hunter drove himself home after the attack and was transported to Benefis Hospital by private vehicle for treatment," the release said.

Officials added that the man sustained "significant but fortunately not life-threatening injuries."

Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks have now confirmed that the bear was a grizzly.

Wildlife officials said Tuesday they used bear hair and tracks to confirm the species.

GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL

Investigators also found the carcass of a domestic cow about 150 yards away.

The man is said to be 20 years old and was taken to the hospital on Monday, according to Lewis and Clark County Sheriff Leo Dutton, as reported by KRTV in Great Falls. 

The man fell into a fetal position during the bear's attack, Dutton said. 

The bear "smacked him around and left," according to Dutton and the same outlet.

Another person wrote that bears "are out. They are fattening up for winter. Heads up, hunters and fishermen."

Still another said, "He is lucky to be alive." 

In a statement, Montana FWP said that its main priority is human safety, and officials urge hunters to retrieve meat as quickly as possible and properly hang anything left behind.

"Avoid cutting up [a] carcass at dusk or night," officials added.

"If you kill an animal at dusk, be prepared to cut up the carcass in the dark by carrying strong headlamps. Be extra vigilant and watch for bears."

State officials also said that, if hunters must leave animals, "return to the site carefully."

"Leave it in an area that is easily observable from a distance," Montana FWP said.

"If a bear has claimed your animal, do not attempt to haze or frighten the bear away. Report any lost game to FWP."

In May, a hiker in Montana survived a terrifying grizzly bear attack on the Grinnell Glacier Trail in Glacier National Park.

item.title: Carnegie Mellon promises 'swift action' against professor Uju Anya over social media posts
item.description: Carnegie Mellon says Uju Anya's social media posts violated community standards, as colleagues report fearing for their safety after being doxxed.
item.content:encoded:
Carnegie Mellon University said Monday it is taking "swift action" after determining that professor Uju Anya’s recent social media posts violated university community standards, with some of her colleagues reporting that they now fear for their personal safety.

President Farnam Jahanian and Provost James H. Garrett Jr. said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital that Anya used "expletives, racial slurs and derogatory language that demeaned, dehumanized and intimidated," while using her Carnegie Mellon affiliation and implying support from university colleagues.

"Carnegie Mellon University is a place where rigorous inquiry, freedom of expression and mutual respect must coexist," their statement read. "We take that responsibility seriously, and we strongly reject language that is hateful and disparages or calls for the harm of others. Such rhetoric is inconsistent with the dignity, respect and responsibility that we expect from one another."

"Dr. Anya’s choice of language violates our shared community standards and distracts from the seriousness and significance of CMU’s scholarship in the humanities and social sciences," the statement added.

REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR

The university also noted that, "Dr. Anya is on voluntary professional leave through summer 2027 and is not teaching classes for CMU this academic year."

Anya, an associate professor at Carnegie Mellon, wrote on X, as the anniversary of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk's assassination was nearing, "They began already, and it ain’t even Kirkmas kirk mubarak, y’all!"

Her X account now appears to be deleted.

Another post from Anya appeared to read, "Die first, White man, and then ask yourself why I am dancing."

Anya is described on her bio page for Carnegie Mellon University as "a scholar of language learning and Black experiences in multilingualism," whose "primary fields of inquiry include critical applied linguistics, critical sociolinguistics and critical discourse studies, with a focus on how race, gender, sexual and social class identities intersect with language learning."

30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS

Carnegie Mellon said university leaders met with faculty and administrators over the weekend, during which employees raised concerns about their safety after being doxxed and receiving threatening messages. Campus police are monitoring the situation but have not found any credible threats to the university, according to CMU.

The university president and chief academic officer promised "swift action in accordance with our processes. We continue to prioritize support for impacted community members, including our students."

INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES

The Carnegie Mellon College Republicans are demanding that Anya be fired, writing in part in a Sunday letter, "Anya’s recent comments are not the first time she has been delighted in the death of others. In 2022, during the final hours of Queen Elizabeth II’s life, Anya posted on X, ‘May her pain be excruciating.’ The backlash to this post was so severe that Carnegie Mellon publicly distanced itself from her comments."

"Friday's posts demonstrate a clear pattern of behavior, one that does not match the conduct expected of a professor at an institution of higher education," the group added.

Fox News Digital reached out to Anya for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Trump-backed crypto bill fails to launch as Dems, Republicans unite to block it
item.description: Sen. Cynthia Lummis declared the Clarity Act dead after Democrats and some Republicans blocked the massive crypto regulation bill in a key Senate vote.
item.content:encoded:
A colossal crypto regulatory package backed by President Donald Trump stumbled in the Senate, and another shot is unlikely.

The Clarity Act failed to move through a key procedural hurdle on Tuesday, serving proponents of the bill, including major players in the cryptocurrency industry and the White House, a major blow in their pursuit of folding the novel currency into the nation’s web of financial regulations.

Democrats dealt the bill a mortal blow, but a handful of Republicans with outstanding concerns, including Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and Jerry Moran, R-Kan., were not assuaged, either. And with little time left on the Senate’s calendar and major bills piling up ahead of the midterm elections, the bill’s biggest backers believed that the Clarity Act might end up back on the shelf.

REPUBLICANS TARGET TRUMP'S CRYPTO EMPIRE WITH NEW PLAN, DEMS SAY IT FALLS SHORT

"I think we're done. It's over," Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., the bill’s primary architect, said. "Because we've been working on this bill for over a year. And we've given them over 120 of their requests and that’s enough."

When asked if the bill would come back to the floor, Lummis said, "Nope."

A midnight hour update was made to the bill to try and pull anyone on the fence off to at least let the package move forward. But it wasn’t enough. And negotiations ran until the very end, just before the vote opened. 

DEMOCRATS HAND TRUMP ONE POWER THEY SPENT YEARS FIGHTING

The issues with the package were many and varying among Democrats and Republicans. Several Senate Democrats were not satisfied with the ethics language baked into the Clarity Act that sought to slow the Trump family’s rapidly growing crypto empire.

That’s because Trump’s income between 2024 and 2025 erupted by about 250% — from just over $620 million to about $2.2 billion.

And much of that increase is attributed to his various holdings and ventures in crypto, which are run by his sons, Don Jr. and Eric, according to the president’s financial disclosure forms reviewed by Fox News Digital.

"We could talk a lot about it," Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., said of his vote against the bill. "But the simple thing is, it allows the corruption of the president to continue."

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., who was working with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., to strengthen the ethics provision in the package, told Fox News Digital, "We were actually getting very, very close, and at the last minute, the banking staffer from [Sen. Tim] Scott's office came in and just said, ‘negotiations are over.’"

"And so, I don't know what happened. You know, we were getting to the point where we were probably going to be able to pass, at least get the motion to proceed, move forward, and then, again, an ethics amendment vote," Gallego said. 

"But I think they got scared with the fact that they had to take an ethics amendment vote. And that's why they killed it. They pulled it at that last minute, so it's bulls---. We were negotiating at the end. At the end of the day, they cared more about protecting the president's right to grift than trying to get a good bill on digital currency."

Others didn’t believe that the language dealing with foreign money laundering had enough teeth.

"I have not seen the kind of engagement yet from the Republican side when it comes to countering terrorist financing and cartel financing that would get me to a yes," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said. "I'm still engaged. I didn't get on board with the GENIUS Act till the very last vote."

TRUMP'S $5,000 DIVIDEND CHECKS WOULD COME WITH A MAJOR CATCH UNDER GOP SENATOR'S PLAN

Still, some lawmakers argued they should at least move forward with the bill to tweak it as needed.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, was still undecided before the vote. He was worried about how bringing crypto into the fold could affect deposit yields at community banks and guardrails on the currency being "diverted for criminal purposes," but he argued the bill could be strengthened if they moved forward.

"What we used to do around here is something called legislate," Cornyn said. "You know where you'd actually vote to get on the bill, but then you amend it, and then you decide whether you're going to support it on the back end."

The bill’s failure does open up the Senate to speedily move to other legislative priorities, like Sen. Ted Cruz's, R-Texas, college sports bill to add protections to student-athletes and slow the big money train ripping through collegiate athletics.

"We committed to ensure that we got a vote on college sports," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "So we'll see if we have 60 [votes]. I don't know the answer for sure to that yet. I hope we do."
